newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's red chip move sensible, discounted-analysts.
newsitem.headline: China's red chip move sensible, discounted-analysts.

text.p: China's efforts to tighten its grip on red chips may weigh on the stocks in the short term, but the Hong Kong market has mostly discounted the move which is ultimately a sensible one, analysts said on Saturday.
"It will cool down some of the speculative fever but it was understood that China would implement some form of measures," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.

China's State Council said on Friday that Chinese-controlled companies making share offers abroad must obtain approval from domestic regulators. Government approval would be required for asset transfers to Chinese-controlled companies abroad if the purpose was to inject the assets into a listed vehicle.
"It was going to happen sooner or later," said Geoff Galbraith, institutional sales trader at NAVA SC Securities.
"The aim is to control their assets."
Red chips -- Hong Kong-based companies with financial backing from China -- have surged this year on expectations that parent companies will inject valuable assets into the companies.

A steady flow of red chip initial public offerings (IPO) has been met with enthusiasm, with the recent offering of Beijing Enterprises Holdings Ltd smashing IPO records in the territory with an oversubscription rate of 1,276 times.
The prospects of slower asset injection growth for red chip companies could hurt sentiment in the short term but analysts said major red chip companies would probably not be affected.

"For the red chips which have less support from their parent companies perhaps it will pose problems for upcoming asset injections," said Patrick Chia, research director at China Everbright Research. "But giant red chips have good connections with the Beijing authorities and will face less problems."
Sunny Chan, senior research manager at Seapower Securities, said regulated asset injections could mean that companies may receive better quality assets. "That will protect investors."

Analysts said it was a sensible move for Beijing to have tighter control over mainland assets and ensure that red chip companies did not accumulate too many assets at too cheap a price which they eventually would be unable to manage.

"It might cool this frenzied buying on red chips and the euphoria might wane because of this but if the company does get final approval its shares will be snapped up right away," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International.
"This news actually has been discounted over the last two months. Investors are fully prepared for this announcement."
Expectations of a move by Beijing prompted a shakeout in red chip stocks in April and just recently, China's ban on state banks trading in stocks prompted more red chip weakness.

But Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities, said investor demand for exposure to China's economy remained strong and slowing the supply of red chips on to the market would only accentuate the focus on existing stocks.
"The party is not over. What Beijing is doing is controlling the supply but they have not reduced the demand," he said.
Analysts said with only 10 days to go before Hong Kong's return to China, they were surprised by Beijing's timing.

They had expected China to move after the handover but said it had chosen to move before a red chip meltdown became imminent. "There is a frenzy over buying red chips. It is just like a bubble -- if there is no regulation the bubble will burst. With more regulations it will be healthier," said Chia.
"With stricter regulations hopefully share prices can correct to a reasonable level," he said.
Chan said China may have also wanted to avoid a sharp drop in share prices after it resumes control of Hong Kong on July 1.
"If the market goes down they lose face."
